analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from permanently replacing workers who exercise their right to strike.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate vote: after hearings in June 1990, it sat in committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, an employer can hire permanent replacements for employees who go on strike, and those replacements can keep the jobs even after the strike ends. This bill would make that an unfair labor practice under the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act, so striking workers could not be permanently displaced for exercising their legally protected rights. It never received a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who strike or engage in other protected union activity would keep their jobs when the dispute ends, instead of losing them permanently to replacement workers. This covers both private-sector workers under the National Labor Relations Act and railroad and airline workers under the Railway Labor Act.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to offer or grant permanent replacement employee status to anyone performing bargaining unit work during a labor dispute [S2] [S3].

Bars employers from giving any hiring or job preference to people who worked, or said they were willing to work, during a labor dispute, over employees who exercised their collective bargaining rights and have returned to work or unconditionally offered to return [S2] [S3].
Applies the same ban to railroads and airlines under the Railway Labor Act, covering their employees' disputes as well [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially in unionized industries, would lose their ability to permanently replace strikers, which they use as leverage to end strikes and to keep operating during one. Any worker willing to cross a picket line could no longer be hired permanently in place of a striker.

drawbacks.text: The permanent-replacement threat is one of the main economic pressures employers can use to bring a strike to an end and keep the business running during a long dispute. Banning it, as this bill would, removes that pressure and could lead to longer strikes, which cost striking workers income in the meantime [S3].

The bill bars any employment preference for replacement workers even after a dispute ends, which employers argue ties their hands in staffing decisions and could leave them short of workers if many strikers do not return [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects a right that federal law already guarantees on paper: the right to strike without losing your job. The cost falls on employers, who lose a powerful tool for ending strikes, and on any worker who wants to take a striker's job permanently. Longer strikes are the real downside for workers themselves, but the bill's core change is to stop an employer from permanently eliminating a striker's job, which most striking workers and unions would see as a clear gain.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and its Labor Subcommittee, which held hearings in June 1990 but never voted to send it to the full Senate, and the Congress ended in January 1991 with no action.

narrative.text: Senator Metzenbaum introduced the bill on February 8, 1990, joined by Senators Kennedy, Adams, and Mikulski, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1] [S5].
Twenty senators signed on as cosponsors, 19 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
On February 20, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor, where hearings were held on June 6, 1990 [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill was never reported out of committee and never received a vote in the Senate before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers came out ahead. Because the bill died in committee, employers kept the right to permanently replace striking workers, and workers who strike kept facing the risk of losing their jobs for good.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chaired the Senate Labor Subcommittee that held its only hearings.

for.name: Sens. Edward Kennedy, William Adams, and Barbara Mikulski
for.role: U.S. Senators (D-MA, D-WA, D-MD), original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined Metzenbaum in introducing the bill on day one.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Labor Subcommittee and never reported it to the full Senate, so it never reached a vote.

against.name: Employer groups opposed to a permanent-replacement ban
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation to ban permanent striker replacement, arguing it would strip employers of their main leverage to end strikes and keep operating during one.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic: 19 of 55 Senate Democrats cosponsored, compared with just 1 of 45 Senate Republicans.

industries.industry: Unionized employers (manufacturing, transportation, airlines, and other strike-prone industries)
industries.note: Employers would lose the right to permanently replace workers who strike, removing their main tool for ending strikes and keeping operations running during a dispute. Workers keep their jobs when a strike ends, which is the direct cost to employers.
The bill amends the Railway Labor Act with the same ban, so carriers could no longer grant permanent replacement status during a craft or class dispute.
The bill removes the threat of permanent replacement, the single biggest deterrent to striking under federal law, making the right to strike meaningful again.
